title: Working with text
summary: Strings are rows of characters: read them by position, change case, split them into words and join them back.

sections.heading: A row of characters
body: A string works a lot like an array of characters: it has a length, and you can read one character by its index.

sections.heading: Strings never change
body: Methods like `toUpperCase` or `upper` do not change the string. They give you a new one, so you have to keep the result.

javascript.code:
let name = 'ada'
name.toUpperCase()
console.log(name)
name = name.toUpperCase()
console.log(name)

python.code:
name = 'ada'
name.upper()
print(name)
name = name.upper()
print(name)

sections.heading: Split into words, join them back
body: `split` cuts a string into a list of pieces; `join` glues a list back into one string.
Watch the spaces. In JavaScript, `split(' ')` turns two spaces in a row into an empty word. `trim()` and `split(/\s+/)` handle that. Python's `split()` with no argument already does.

javascript.code:
const line = ' red  green blue'
console.log(line.split(' '))
const words = line.trim().split(/\s+/)
console.log(words)
console.log(words.join('-'))

python.code:
line = ' red  green blue'
print(line.split(' '))
words = line.split()
print(words)
print('-'.join(words))

sections.heading: Checking what a character is
body: To keep only letters or digits, test each character. A regular expression works in both languages; Python also has handy methods like `isalpha` and `isalnum`.

typescript.code:
const isLetter = (ch: string): boolean => /[a-z]/i.test(ch)
console.log(isLetter('q'), isLetter('7'))

mistakes: Comparing before lowercasing: `'A'` and `'a'` are different characters.
Calling a method and forgetting to keep its result.
Splitting on a single space when the text can contain several.
